title: Infosys Sees No Material Impact From US Suspension of PERM Program
excerpt: India's second-largest IT firm told stock exchanges on Saturday that the Labor Department's freeze on green-card labor certifications would not affect it materially, even as the suspension stalls thousands of immigrant worker cases across eight tech companies.
body:
• Infosys said on Saturday, Oct. 10, that it does not expect a material impact from the U.S. Department of Labor's suspension of its PERM green-card filings.
  • On Oct. 8, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, alongside Vice President JD Vance, suspended eight firms — Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe — from the Permanent Labor Certification program amid federal fraud investigations. New filings are refused; pending cases are frozen with no end date.
  • What it means for you: if your employer is one of the eight, no new PERM case can start and pending cases sit idle — but H-1B status, extensions and existing work authorization are unaffected. Workers nearing the six-year H-1B limit should consult their employer's immigration counsel, since the 365-day PERM filing clock that unlocks extensions cannot start during the suspension.
  • Federal records show Infosys had 13 PERM decisions in fiscal 2025 and zero frozen cases. The stalled pipeline sits mostly with Microsoft (about 1,600 frozen cases) and Adobe (about 560).

Infosys has brushed off one of Washington's sharpest escalations yet against foreign-worker programs. India's second-largest IT services firm said on Saturday that it does not anticipate a material impact from the suspension of its Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) filings, two days after the U.S. Department of Labor barred eight major technology companies from the program that underpins employer-sponsored green cards.

Context & Background

PERM is the Department of Labor's certification that no qualified, willing U.S. worker is available for a job before an employer sponsors a foreign national for permanent residency — typically EB-2 and EB-3 green cards. It is the mandatory first step before the immigrant petition reaches U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The suspension was announced on Oct. 8 at a White House briefing led by Sonderling and Vance, under the administration's Anti-Fraud Task Force initiative. Sonderling said the department would "not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications" involving the eight firms, adding that they had collectively requested nearly three million foreign workers since 2009 and received over 230,000 H-1B approvals and 100,000 permanent labor certifications.

Impact & Analysis

For the Indian IT services firms, the business risk looks limited — they had already walked away from PERM. Labor Department disclosure records show Cognizant had zero PERM decisions from October 2024 through June 2026, and Infosys just 13. TCS filed one batch of about 510 cases in early 2024 and almost nothing since. Nasscom argued the path from H-1B to permanent residency through PERM is relatively limited at its members.

The real pipeline exposure sits at the two U.S. majors: an estimated 1,600 frozen Microsoft cases and about 560 at Adobe, out of about 3,200 stalled cases across all eight firms. The main channel of fallout may be voluntary attrition — workers with frozen cases moving to employers that can still sponsor.

Crucially, this is a PERM suspension, not an H-1B ban. H-1B petitions, extensions and existing work authorization at the eight firms are untouched.

"We welcome the opportunity to work with the Department of Labor and related government agencies to answer any questions they may have."

— Infosys, in a stock exchange filing

Diaspora Angle

The human cost concentrates on workers mid-pipeline, and Indian nationals — who face the longest green-card backlogs of any nationality — are hit hardest. An H-1B holder can extend past year six only if a PERM or immigrant petition was filed at least 365 days earlier; employees at the suspended firms with no PERM on file cannot start that clock while the freeze lasts. And with the Department of Labor's PERM review already averaging about 336 days, lost filing time will not be recovered quickly even if the suspension lifts.

What's Next

No end date was given. Analysts say the likely legal authority allows a hold during a fraud investigation for 180 days initially — putting the first natural review point around April 6, 2027. Vance said the list "could apply to a number of other technology companies," keeping the sector on watch. For Infosys and its peers, the next signal is whether the investigations conclude quickly — and whether Washington's crackdown stops at labor certification or reaches further into the visa programs the Indian IT industry depends on.
